specPoints.text: describe the qualitative variation of resistance of light-dependent resistors (LDRs) with illumination and thermistors with temperature
know that lamps and LEDs can be used to indicate the presence of a current in a circuit

primer.text: Some resistors respond to the world around them: warmth thins a thermistor's resistance, brightness thins an LDR's. Others simply announce that a current is flowing. This note covers thermistors and light-dependent resistors as sensors, then lamps and LEDs as the circuit's built-in current indicators.

lessons.title: Thermistors & LDRs
lessons.opening: Two components turn the physical world into resistance readings. The thermistor watches the temperature; the LDR watches the light. Both follow the same pattern — more of their condition means less resistance — and both plot it as a falling curve. This lesson maps each sensor's behaviour and its graph.
keyPoints: A thermistor's resistance depends on its temperature.
Thermistors read high in the cold and low in the heat.
Warming a thermistor lowers its resistance; cooling it raises the resistance.
An LDR's resistance depends on the light intensity falling on it.
LDRs read high in darkness and low in bright light.
Both devices plot resistance against their condition as a falling curve.

low.restatement: Thermistor: hot means low resistance, cold means high. LDR: bright means low resistance, dark means high.
low.analogy: Two lazy guards: the more activity around them (heat or light), the less they block the way.
low.examPointer: Anchor each answer with the pair — condition and resistance — e.g. 'hot thermistor, low resistance'.

medium.restatement: The resistance-to-condition graph falls for both sensors, which is why they excel at threshold circuits: crossing a temperature or light level swings the resistance sharply.
medium.analogy: Automatic streetlights: darkness raises the LDR's resistance until the sensing circuit flips the lamp on.
medium.examPointer: The graphs show an inverse-style curve — quote 'high in cold/dark, low in hot/bright' and the graph shape together.

check.stem: As a thermistor warms up, its resistance:

options.explanation: Heat lowers the thermistor's resistance, not raises it.
Hot conditions give a thermistor its low resistance.
Responding to temperature is the thermistor's whole job.
The response is smooth and repeatable.

check.stem: In dark conditions, an LDR's resistance is:

options.explanation: Low resistance belongs to bright light.
Darkness sends the LDR's resistance up.
The resistance rises in the dark but never reaches zero.

options.text: the same as in bright light
options.explanation: Responding to light is the LDR's whole job.

check.stem: Which component responds to light intensity?

options.explanation: The thermistor watches temperature.
A fixed resistor ignores its surroundings by design.
The light-dependent resistor tracks the light intensity on it.
The diode's job is direction control, not sensing.

check.stem: Brighter light shining on an LDR, at a fixed voltage, makes the current through it:

options.explanation: Brighter light lowers the resistance, which raises the current.

options.text: larger, because the resistance has dropped
options.explanation: Less opposition at the same push means more flow.
The LDR's changing resistance must move the current.
More light never blocks the current.

check.stem: The resistance-temperature graph of a thermistor is:

options.explanation: A horizontal line would mean unchanging resistance.
Resistance falls with temperature, so nothing rises.
The graph dives as temperature climbs — the inverse-style curve.
A vertical line would mean the temperature reading is impossible.

check.stem: State how a thermistor's resistance changes between cold and hot conditions.
check.modelAnswer: It is high when cold and low when hot — raising the temperature lowers the resistance.

check.stem: State how an LDR's resistance responds to bright and dark conditions.
check.modelAnswer: High in the dark and low in bright light — more illumination means less resistance.

check.stem: Explain why an LDR suits an automatic night light.
check.modelAnswer: When darkness falls the LDR's resistance rises sharply, so the circuit can sense the change and switch the lamp on; in daylight the low resistance reverses the behaviour.

check.stem: A thermistor sits in a fridge sensor circuit at a fixed voltage. When the fridge cools, what happens to the thermistor's resistance and to the current through it?
check.modelAnswer: Cooling raises the thermistor's resistance, so the current through it falls.

lessons.title: Lamps & LEDs
lessons.opening: A circuit can report on itself. Fit a lamp or an LED where you want to watch, and its glow certifies that current is flowing — and for an LED, which way. This lesson covers the two indicators and the one-way rule that makes the LED so telling.
keyPoints: Lamps and LEDs light up when a current flows through them.
That makes both useful as indicators of a current's presence in a circuit.
An LED is a diode, so it passes current in one direction only.
An LED lights only when placed the correct way round in the circuit.

low.restatement: If it glows, current is flowing — that is the whole trick behind lamps and LEDs as indicators.
low.analogy: A pilot light on a stove: the glow is the proof that the gas (current) is actually on.
low.examPointer: Answer indicator questions with the pair: component lights up, therefore current present.

medium.restatement: The LED doubles as a direction probe: being a diode, it lights only when wired the conducting way, so darkness after a rebuild points to reversal.
medium.analogy: A one-way turnstile with a bell: you hear it (see the glow) only when people pass the permitted way.
medium.examPointer: Two arrows away from a symbol mean light-emitting; two arrows towards it mean light-dependent. Learn the arrow rule.

check.stem: Lamps and LEDs can indicate the presence of:

options.explanation: Components do not glow in proportion to resistance.
The glow tracks the current flowing, not the voltage alone.
Both light up exactly when current flows through them.
The indicator reads the circuit's flow, not the cell's reserve.

check.stem: A light-emitting diode (LED) is which component type?

options.explanation: Thermistors sense temperature; LEDs emit light.
Meters measure; LEDs indicate and emit.
Capacitors store charge — a different family entirely.
LED stands for light-emitting diode.

check.stem: An LED fails to light when:

options.explanation: Steady current lights an LED as well as any.

options.text: it is wired in the reverse direction
options.explanation: Reversed, the diode blocks and the LED stays dark.
Copper wiring is the normal, conducting choice.
Smoothness of supply has no bearing on the LED's glow.

check.stem: On a circuit symbol, two arrows pointing away from the component mean it is:

options.explanation: Arrows towards a symbol mean light-dependent.
Arrows radiating away mean the component emits light.
Temperature sensing has its own symbol conventions.
Meters are drawn in circles without emission arrows.

check.stem: Which pair both glow to show a current is flowing?

options.explanation: Both illuminate when current passes, so both serve as indicators.
Meters read quantities; they do not glow as indicators.
Sensors respond to the world; they do not announce current by glowing.
Neither the supply nor the switch glows with the current.

check.stem: Name two components that light up to show a current is present.
check.modelAnswer: Lamps and light-emitting diodes (LEDs) both illuminate when current flows.

check.stem: Which way must an LED face to light up, and why?
check.modelAnswer: In the forward direction — an LED is a diode, so current passes one way only.

check.stem: Explain why an LED makes a reliable indicator of current direction as well as presence.
check.modelAnswer: The LED lights only when current flows through it the permitted way, so a lit LED certifies both that a current exists and that it runs the right way round.

check.stem: A student builds a circuit with an LED that stays dark. The battery and resistor are fine. Suggest the likely fault and the fix.
check.modelAnswer: The LED is probably reversed — being a diode it conducts one way only, so turning it around in the circuit should let the current flow and the LED glow.

glossary.definition: A temperature-sensing resistor — high resistance in the cold, low in the heat.
A light-sensing resistor — high resistance in darkness, low in bright light.
How much light falls on a surface — the condition an LDR responds to.
The brightness landing on the LDR; more illumination means less resistance.
A diode that glows when current passes the permitted direction.
A component that conducts in one direction only.
